title: Λέων ⟨μῦν φοβηθεὶς⟩ καὶ ἀλώπηξ
titleEn: The Lion Frightened by a Mouse, and the Fox
part: The Lion Frightened by a Mouse, and the Fox (Chambry 213)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 213. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέοντος κοιμωμένου μῦς τὸ σῶμα διέδραμεν.
sentences.tr: Leontos koimōmenou mys to sōma diedramen.
sentences.l: A lion sleeping, a mouse ran-across his body.
sentences.i: While a lion slept, a mouse ran across his body.
sentences.n: Two words make a genitive absolute, λέοντος κοιμωμένου, and they carry the whole opening scene. διατρέχω takes the accusative of the ground covered. Fable 206 opens with almost these same words — the collection keeps two versions of the sleeping lion and the mouse, and they end quite differently.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἐξαναστὰς πανταχόθεν περιειλίττετο ζητῶν τὸν προσεληλυθότα.
sentences.tr: Ho de exanastas pantachothen perieilitteto zētōn ton proselēlythota.
sentences.l: And he, having-started-up, kept-twisting-himself-about on every side, seeking the one who had-come-upon-him.
sentences.i: He started up and turned himself about every way, looking for whatever had come at him.
sentences.n: περιειλίττομαι in the middle is to wind oneself round — the lion twisting to inspect his own flanks. τὸν προσεληλυθότα is a perfect participle used as a noun, "the one who has come up": the lion does not yet know what it was, and the Greek keeps him in the dark by naming no animal.

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ δὲ αὐτὸν θεασαμένη ὠνείδιζεν, εἰ λέων ὢν μῦν ηὐλαβήθη.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx de auton theasamenē ōneidizen, ei leōn ōn myn ēulabēthē.
sentences.l: And a fox, having-seen him, kept-reproaching him, that, being a lion, he had-taken-fright at a mouse.
sentences.i: A fox saw him and jeered at him for having, lion though he was, gone in fear of a mouse.
sentences.n: εἰ after a verb of reproach or of emotion is not "if" but "that, because" — Greek states the ground of the feeling as a supposition. λέων ὤν is concessive: though he was a lion. εὐλαβέομαι is to be wary of, to shrink from, a milder word than φοβέομαι, which the lion himself will use in his reply.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὃς ἀπεκρίνατο· « Οὐ τὸν μῦν ἐφοβήθην, ἐθαύμασα δὲ εἴ τις λέοντος κοιμωμένου τὸ σῶμα ἐπιδραμεῖν ἐτόλμησεν. »
sentences.tr: Kai hos apekrinato· « Ou ton myn ephobēthēn, ethaumasa de ei tis leontos koimōmenou to sōma epidramein etolmēsen. »
sentences.l: And he answered: « I did not fear the mouse; but I wondered that anyone had-dared to run-over the body of a lion sleeping. »
sentences.i: And he answered: « It was not the mouse I feared; I wondered that anyone should dare to run over the body of a sleeping lion. »
sentences.n: Καὶ ὅς, "and he", is the old demonstrative use of the relative pronoun, kept alive in this fixed phrase at the head of a reply. εἰ again means "that" after a verb of wondering. λέοντος κοιμωμένου comes back word for word from the first sentence, but no longer standing free: here it hangs on τὸ σῶμα, the body of a sleeping lion. That is how the lion shifts the marvel from the mouse's size to the mouse's nerve.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος διδάσκει τοὺς φρονίμους τῶν ἀνθρώπων μηδὲ τῶν μετρίων πραγμάτων καταφρονεῖν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos didaskei tous phronimous tōn anthrōpōn mēde tōn metriōn pragmatōn kataphronein.
sentences.l: The story teaches the prudent among men not to despise even slight matters.
sentences.n: καταφρονέω takes the genitive of what is looked down on. μηδέ is "not even", the negative μή belonging to the infinitive after a verb of teaching. τὰ μέτρια are things of moderate size — the middling, the unimpressive.
